chapters.title: Welcome and how the debate works
What each would do differently as a senator
Who is responsible for the divide between parties
Anything in your personal past to address
Audience question: medication costs and mental health

turns.speaker: Angel Zierden
paragraphs: Alright, well thank you guys for being here and everyone that's joining us online. I'm the CEO and founder of Alethical. My name is Angel Zierden. We run an intelligence inside our political data, campaign, finance, and legislation to be able to give all of you guys information that you wouldn't normally have had. I'm really excited to host this debate. I admire both of these guys for stepping up and running. I admire their friendship as well. And for this debate, there are no rules. They have not received the questions beforehand. They do not know what I said. [unclear] I was going to ask them our questions, so I have to do that. And I expect just basic form, right? If you want to reply, just say you would like to reply, and you can reply and hopefully we [unclear] have a really, really good discussion. Trent Dilks, Aaron Brutger, SD13. So we, will actually, before we start, they both joined the Forward Coalition. So the Forward Independence Party in Minnesota was formerly the independent party that emerged and one of the reasons for starting that coalition was that we wanted to make it the gold standard that every candidate be cross-endorsed or join the coalition for the independent party to basically tell voters, hey, when I go down to the Capitol, it doesn't matter if I'm sitting across the aisle from somebody who disagrees with me on the other side. We are going to sit down and we are going to talk. Just like our founding fathers did, we expect that that [unclear] the new gold standard in the state of Minnesota today. So we will go ahead and get started.

turns.speaker: Angel Zierden
paragraphs: So I will ask you to go ahead and introduce yourself as a person, family, community, and whatever else you'd like to share.

turns.speaker: Aaron Brutger
paragraphs: All right. My name is Aaron Brutger, and I am going to be your voice in the Minnesota Senate, representing Minnesota Senate District 13. I am a write-in candidate. As you know, the campaign did not start that way. I earned the endorsement of the Senate District 13 Republicans overwhelmingly on the first ballot back this spring. And things were going pretty well for a while. However, a few folks decided that they did not want me to be the candidate with the R by my name, so they found someone to run against me in the primary.

He was backed by a lot of independent expenditures and ultimately did win the primary. After the primary, I received calls, texts, emails, messages from many, many folks who were really disgusted with what happened in our district, and they were encouraging me to do a write-in. I initially declined, but after the calls kept coming in and hearing that folks were planning on sitting out, I didn't know what else I could do [unclear] throw my name in as a write-in. I have worked with the Senate District 13 Republicans since 2012. I chaired the district from 2017 through 2023, and one of my main goals has been to get as many people involved in the process as possible, and to be honest, regardless of political [unclear] Any of you that know me, I will talk to absolutely anybody. I'm a process guy and when I chaired my first convention, I realized that a lot of people are not familiar with Roberts Rules of Order. So I took it upon myself to condense that roughly 700 page book into a little cheat sheet and I have handed out thousands of them. Our Republic does not work unless people participate and are educated in the process. And again, regardless of political leanings, I really, I don't care. Just get involved, stay involved. And actually, I did bring copies of that [unclear]-sheet. So again, regardless of your political leanings, if you want a copy of it, feel free to take one [unclear] at that back table over there. We need as many people involved as possible. I am married. I have four kids. I'm the director of product and technology for an [unclear] company based [unclear] Minnesota. And yeah, I'm self-taught and voting. I'm the front hand of the band. I play a whole bunch of different instruments. And I'm kind of a political junkie, I guess.

turns.speaker: [speaker uncertain]
paragraphs: There you go. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Trent Dilks
paragraphs: Hi, I'm Trent Dilks. I am a father of four. We have two six-year-olds, a five and a one, so mostly I'm tired. The one-year-old the other night got me up at 4 a .m. And I still haven't quite recovered from that. So exhaustion is just kind of a constant state right now. I'm a two-tour operation Iraqi Freedom veteran. I was a machine gunner on my first tour in 05-07. And then as we were shutting our rack down, I went back just to make sure I don't enjoy the Middle East. I confirmed it, I do not. I'm not built for the weather there. So I got out of the Minnesota National Guard after 10 years. Got my degree in political science and then I went to work as a veterans advocate, advocating for veterans, their families and survivors. For the past 13 years I've worked for a non-profit doing exactly that work. I've worked a lot in St. Paul, a few accomplishments, the first ever veterans [unclear] the [unclear] in Minnesota five years ago, I led the fight for that. It used to be that veterans legislation got tossed into a bunch of partisan garbage. And then it would be used to embarrass your opponent or the other side. You put a poison pill in there when you knew somebody couldn't support And you'd also toss in a veterans piece. And then you [unclear] point and go, look, so-and-so doesn't support veterans. Everybody knew it was bullshit, but it was a game that they were enjoying playing. Five years ago, they weren't going to pass anything. I know, hard to believe. And I went down to the Capitol with a thousand of my closest friends and called for the veterans to finally be taken out of the partisan mess and the passage of the first veterans omnibus bill. They quoted a lot of rules. They had a lot of excuses. We just kept counting them, and lo and behold, they were [unclear] the suspended rules nearly unanimously. There's one law major in St. Paul, I can't remember his name now, but he is there just to vote against everything. As long as he never votes for anything, they'll keep sending him back. He was in the House. He was the only vote in the House and [unclear] against him. A couple months ago, we had the fifth ever veterans omnibus bill. So lasting change in all the politics and legislation for veterans and families and survivors are done in Minnesota. I've worked on a lot of issues and I've worked with everybody. I've also been let down by everybody. 13 years of doing that kind of work and it really lifts up the cover of how things work or don't work there. That's what eventually pushed me into this. I had a bill to help our most severely disabled veterans get some property tax relief. It hadn't been done for 19 years. I don't know if you all have property taxes you pay, but what happened to them over the last 19 years. Well we haven't adjusted that for the most severely disabled veterans or the surviving spouses of those who died in or as a result of their service. It's a fight I've been having for a long time. Tied House, so I had a Democrat and a Republican introduce the exact same bill. Not a single word different. They got hurt on the same day in the House and one was presented and one side sat on their hands, the other one presented, the other side sat on their hands and that's broken. That's broken. It doesn't matter. Whose name was at the top of it, who authored it, it didn't matter. We were trying to do something right for our most severely disabled veterans, those who [unclear] paid the highest possible, [unclear] life, not responsible price for their service, and they couldn't set that aside for one vote. And that was the tipping point for me. It's like, okay, I really love the work I'm doing, but we need some people that are going to talk common sense and say, this was the right thing. The room wasn't filled with bad people. There were some great lawmakers, but they're stuck in a really bad system. They're stuck in a really tough place where everything is set up to try to keep you in line. I know there are good people in that room. I've worked with them on a lot of things and had a lot of conversations. But what's going on and how that shook out means we have to go back for a 19th year. So it was 18 years for a 19th year to try to get this fixed. And it shouldn't be that way. So that's what motivated me to run among a lot of other reasons but yeah that's why I'm here and I'm glad to be having this discussion thank you very much for hosting this greatly appreciate it

turns.speaker: Angel Zierden
paragraphs: Thank you guys so you both kind of answered the next question a little bit but I will rephrase it since you both kind of have a reason why you're running what is something that you're going to do differently as a senator that no one else is doing in the legislature right now?

turns.speaker: Trent Dilks
paragraphs: [unclear] It's not, let's see, it's not that nobody's doing it. There are people who are able to work across the aisle on certain things. It's that it needs to be magnified. Those people can't feel like they're alone on an island. We have to add more strong, independent voices to that. It's not that everything compromises the right answer to everything, but there are plenty of things where it is the right answer. I have some absolute values that I won't compromise on, things that no matter who proposes them, I'll fight tooth and nail against. But on the things where we can make progress, we should make progress. Zero sum is absolutely destroying us. The win-lose, keeping score, other side is my enemy thing is absolutely ripping us apart. So that would be absolutely the way I would focus is gain ground, work towards the end. It's okay, it's okay as long as it's moving the ball in the right direction to do that kind of work. And even if it's somebody who doesn't have the same party affiliation as you, as long as it's headed in the right direction for the people of Minnesota, cut the crap and get it done.

turns.speaker: Aaron Brutger
paragraphs: I actually agree with Trent on that one. And to take it a step further, Article 4, Section 17 of the Minnesota Constitution requires the single subject clause. We need to get away from omnibus bills. You know, with that, both parties love using them. They love filing as much stuff into a single bill as possible. And then they just vote along party lines, yes or no, or yay or nay. We have to get away from that. It's in our Constitution. It's bad legislation or bad practice to just shove a whole bunch of things that really don't have a whole lot to do with one another into one bill. So standing around on that. There are some folks that are starting to do that but that needs to be the norm so just pushing and standing by that.

turns.speaker: Angel Zierden
paragraphs: All right you guys both joined the former coalition together on the same day at the Capitol. What pushback have you received or what fears did you have going into it about joining that coalition?

turns.speaker: Aaron Brutger
paragraphs: There's been some pushback amongst some of the more hard-nosed GOP votes, which I anticipated. And that's okay. So right after I was endorsed by the Republicans, Trent was endorsed by the Democrats, he held a meeting in this very room actually. And I shot him a message said, hey, I'd like to introduce myself, you know, we can have a quick chat, whatever, I might bring some people and they'll be civil. So I showed up, introduced myself, and Trent and I started chatting. We both agreed to lead by example, and we need civility in politics. We agreed that we would heavily debate policy and our positions on things. But you can disagree with someone and debate without being disrespectful or without getting overly aggressive. Being passionate is great. I mean, a person running for office has to be passionate or why are you even doing this? But civility matters and I can probably say he stuck to that and I stuck to that so when the forward coalition approached it was a no brainer we had already agreed to it many months prior and the fact that the forward independence coalition they're not requiring you to abandon your party or abandon your principles it's just the idea is to provide a better way forward [unclear] civility, maintaining decorum and having positive debate, keeping the best interests of Minnesota at the forefront.

turns.speaker: Trent Dilks
paragraphs: Yeah, I think I actually encouraged you to bring some people in. It was a 10 hour open house in town hall that I held as my first event, because I think that's how you should do these things. You want to represent people, you've got to be available to those people. For joining the Forward Independence Coalition, yeah, there's definitely been some blowback on that. And it was odd to me because from the very beginning, I'm the great candidate. If you've seen my signs, it's got the great back on it. I come from a non-partisan world and I'm extremely uncomfortable with partisan titles. You know, saying we instead of they still does not work very well for me. So I have not, I have never been and I probably never will be a good partisan. It's just, it's not in my genetics. And so, yeah, to me, joining the coalition was pretty simple. It was saying, I will put people over party. That's it.

If you've been to any of my 10 town halls, if you've listened to me ramble at copies or everything that I've shown up to, this shouldn't come as a surprise. I believe genuinely that you put people over party. That that's the job. That's what a representative government like ours means. The great doc is the idea of regionality of what your representatives are supposed to be. A DFL-er from the 13th District should not look like a DFL-er from downtown Minneapolis because they are not being sent to St. Paul by the exact same people. They are representative of the populations that send them. A Republican from Minnesota shouldn't be on the same exact platform as a Republican from Mississippi. It doesn't make sense. One-size-fits-all politics is leaving. So you wouldn't believe how many people have come up to me and told me they feel politically homeless. They don't have a party. They don't have a place where they feel like they belong. And in a representative government, that's bullshit. That is, you should. You should have those things. And the fact that you're in a place and we've got blue box and red box, and now pick which one's the least uncomfortable and cram yourself in it is not something that I think is long-term sustainable unless we're allowed to have a regional identity to those things. And so it was a no-brainer for me to join. It's unfortunate that there was blowback. I understand that it was, you know, not taken well by some and that's okay because I'm not going to change who I am or what I believe in to maybe get some support out of the states or to get whatever might be strings attached to not seeing what you actually believe. That's when it's most important when you know the cost is going to be there and you go ahead and you do it anyway. So I'm proud to have done it. I'm proud to now have the Forward Independence Party's endorsement officially. I interviewed for that. So the one thing that the political parties can agree on is they like the Grey duck. So I carry that in addition to. I love the local DFL. They have absolutely had my back. The members of it, it's not in any way turning on them. It is just saying exactly what I've been saying is we can't have people feeling so good homeless in our system.

turns.speaker: Angel Zierden
paragraphs: So you both have learned a lot this year. I'm gonna go off of script here for a minute. Based on everything that you guys have learned this year, who do you think is responsible for the divide in government and between the two parties, and how do you think we fix it?

turns.speaker: Trent Dilks
paragraphs: I thought I was going to ask a tough question. This is great. What the hell? Let's do it. There's a lot to that. There's a lot to unpack there. I don't want to steal all the thunder from Aaron, so I'll leave at least half the question unanswered. It starts out with a system that truly benefits from keeping us divided. It truly benefits from keeping us apart from one another. When I'm out knocking doors, and I've knocked a lot of doors, think of the most divisive issues that are used to rip us apart. They don't come up on the front doorstep. They do not come up. Affordability. Fraud comes up some, but not as much as the headlines would have you believe when you're at the doorstep. They're worried about healthcare, they're worried about childcare, they're worried about a lot of things that really impact them there at home. And those are things we should be able to work together on. There's a lot of agreement on those things. But as long as you can use a few wedge issues to keep everybody ripped apart, then you're going to continue to be successful. As long as you can use zero-sum politics, good guy, bad guy, enemy, whatever you call it. I'm not even comfortable with an opponent. We should be running for the same thing. Same as an opponent. We should both be trying to get the same job. And it's so disappointing. But there is a lot of interest in making sure that things don't work and we stay divided. There are a lot of ways to exploit a dysfunctional system and not make drastic improvements. And that is a vested interest where you see money in politics actually invested. I've seen through your company where the reports where [unclear] certain people doesn't matter what side you're donating to politicians on both sides right that's not because they're trying to get something done that's because they want influence and no matter who's in power they want to try this way. But it's not ideological it's not trying to move the ball forward it's trying to bring the money back it's trying to accomplish a goal that may not be for the best of the people in [unclear] So there's a lot of answers to that, but I'm going to go with the vested interest in keeping us divided, using a few wedge issues as my answer.

turns.speaker: Aaron Brutger
paragraphs: Yeah, as Trent touched on, the division is what fundraisers for both major parties. You know, I look at the Republican Party, and they've been fundraising for years based off of that, if we could just get a little more money, a few more donations, we could take over the House or the Senate or the Governor's office. It's just the division, it has to stop. It's used to keep us fighting over things that I'm not going to say don't matter because they absolutely do matter. But again, it's not serving we the people. The independent expenditures, the fact that certain organizations can spend unlimited amounts of money on a campaign has to stop. Citizens United getting overturned are huge. Individuals have contribution limits. These PACs, they don't. They can fund whoever they want, and they can pump as much money as they want. In. And with that, I mean, we saw the direct result of that in Senate District 13. It just, the powers that be, as Trent said, want to keep us divided. If they are able to funnel money through these PACs to support their chosen candidates, the thing is, as Trent also stated, these same groups are funding folks on both sides. It is meant for them to maintain control. All of us little guys cannot compete with that and they know it. So until we put a stop to that, I really don't see how things are going to change.

turns.speaker: Angel Zierden
paragraphs: Thank you.

turns.speaker: Angel Zierden
paragraphs: As a former mayor, I know that your personal life can be scrutinized and there are things [unclear] that people can bring up. Is there anything about your past in your personal life that you would like to address now?

turns.speaker: Aaron Brutger
paragraphs: Yeah, so the justification for a number of folks to have someone run against me was based off of an arrest that happened. I have full custody of my two oldest kids. My ex had made some claims. I got arrested. I ended up fighting the charges. I did tell the sheriff that I had yelled at her, so I agreed to plead guilty to disorderly conduct. Less than a year and a half later, I was awarded full custody of my two oldest kids. I was [unclear] court essentially twice and ultimately got custody of my kids. I never went to try to get it expunged because it never affected my employment, my life, whatever. And it's something that happened. You know, going through that, I guess, I'm not sure what future questions there are, but we absolutely need criminal justice reform. I'm [unclear] too far here though, as well as some family court reform. But it's just, it's a shame that that kind of stuff was webinized. I refuse to speak ill of my ex. Ultimately, she's biological on my kids. I didn't do it then. I didn't do it after court. I'm not about to do it when I'm running for office. The fact that that was weaponized is disgusting, and the folks that did should be ashamed of themselves. When I spoke with certain folks in GOP leadership after this came up, I said, look, listen, guys, I was a single dad in the state of Minnesota that got full custody of my two kids. I wasn't married when the kids were born. That is a very, very uphill battle. Courts do not just award custody to the father. And I even pitched to them, we should be fundraising off of this. But instead, some folks decided to amplify it, run to the media with it, and essentially just try to completely destroy my character. I had never [unclear] the fact that an arrest happen. In fact, so I got full custody in August of 2011 and early 2012 is when I got involved in politics. I had approached my state senator at the time and I wanted them to work on changing custody laws based on what I went through. I knew if there was anything I could do to help the next person and family this might affect, I had an obligation to do so. So the fact that this was weaponized against me, [unclear] it was very disgusting.

turns.speaker: Trent Dilks
paragraphs: I was going to tell the plot, you know what you did last summer, but then I remembered that things can be edited and I wasn't actually the convertible that hit a long short. So, no, I really don't have anything. They call me St. Trent. So, no. I was lucky enough that my wild days in my 20s all stayed off of the record, so I'll leave them that way.

turns.speaker: Angel Zierden
paragraphs: Thank you. The next couple questions [unclear] direct towards just one of you and then I'll go to the next person. Let's start with you, Trent. How did your military service shape your approach to politics and what did you see that influences how you look at politics politics and military?

turns.speaker: Trent Dilks
paragraphs: It changed a lot of it. It really did. It's very interesting to have a part of your life and make the decision enlisted when I was 17 years old with a parent's signature. And then a couple of short years later, well actually I think a year later, this place from the 90s Iraq opted to lose. And next thing you know my freshman year of college I am called up and for the next two years I will live Iraq in ways that changed my life. Some for the better, some for the worse, but all because of a decision I made at 17.

And by decisions made by people in Washington and politicians, some spineless, some self-motivated, none of that mattered when I was serving. It was all about the person next to you. And nothing about the person next to you mattered. Their political beliefs, their religious beliefs, their ethnic background. None of that mattered because you were in it together. And I think we need more of that. That's an experience to know that service, on service with those you're with, does not matter. All of the things we use to divide each other mean absolutely nothing when you're in a situation like that. As far as my political views and how I view the world, I am so, you know, I was a gravel road kid. I was, I grew up [unclear] my nearest neighbors were cornfields and hog farms. I worked on hog farms, worked in a meat packing plant to start to go to college before the GI Bill kicked in. And going to another part of the world, experiencing Iraq, the Iraqi people, seeing their lives really was an expansion of my understanding and my concept of what's out there. Also coming back to the United States after seeing people with silverware. The access of our country. And it was a very hard adjustment to make for a while because all of a sudden there's everything everywhere. Everybody wants it now in the slightest inconvenience is the end of the world. And you just kind of for a while you want to shake people. And then later on it just becomes an annoyance. But it really did. It crafted a lot of those things and changed my view and took [unclear] and made me into a [unclear]

turns.speaker: Angel Zierden
paragraphs: As we've seen, some questions for you, Aaron. As we've seen this year, the value of the endorsement from the BPU use has significantly declined based on both sides of the aisle. We saw a lot of people who didn't get the endorsement and then go on to win the primary. In your experience as a [unclear] what did you think about going into it? And then how has that shaped your view of politics? And do you think we should continue on with the endorsement process in Minnesota or move to a primary?

turns.speaker: Aaron Brutger
paragraphs: So I've been involved for a while. And historically, in Senate District 13, we haven't had anything like this happen on the Republican side. At the state level, there's always been some disagreement, but ultimately, the party has backed the endorsed candidates. For one reason or another, this election cycle, it did not go that way. I have the full support of the local Senate District 13 Republicans. They were absolutely great. They're in kind of a tough position right now, but throughout the process they have supported me 100%. In terms of moving forward, I think ideally, [unclear] chaos that happened at the state convention, I think at the local levels, I feel more like House and Senate, we should still do endorsement conventions. Because otherwise, I guess I don't want to speak for Trent, but I highly doubt a person like Trent or myself would ever even be considered. Because at the small levels, it would become whoever has the most money and can buy their way in, advertise their way in. The grassroots efforts matter. They truly do. I would love to say at the state level that they matter. It seems they used to, but with all of the big money involved in how things are going, I think we would be better served if we would move at the state level to an earlier primary and then go from there. But again, at the local level, I would not change a thing. Otherwise, your average person who feels compelled to run to represent their district would never have a shot. [unclear]

turns.speaker: Angel Zierden
paragraphs: To [unclear]

turns.speaker: Trent Dilks
paragraphs: Yeah, and I will point out on the DFL side, I 100 % of the endorsed carried the primary, so they did that 1 ,000. And local endorsement is important. And the process of building that, you know, we all have to do better of making sure more people come in. But I was just talking to somebody at a town hall and they were railing against the fact that we're the young people. And I was tired, I was grumpy. So I answered very directly. A lot of this becomes a luxury, right? Participation in this process, when you're worried about making your mortgage payment, when you're worried about healthcare, when you're worried about all sorts of things, when you're being squeezed from every single direction, it becomes a bit of a luxury to be able to give your time and resources to the process. We have a lot of people who would love to get their voices heard, but they're just trying to make it to tomorrow. And so if we can find a way to try to bring them in earlier in the process, we're all going to be better for it. But I don't hold it against those who can't show up because stuff is hard. Life is hard right now. And they're pulling a lot of directions.

turns.speaker: Angel Zierden
paragraphs: Hey, family Leave. Do you have an opinion on it prior to being implemented? Do you have an opinion on it now? And what do you think needs to change or what should have been done differently during the creation of it and the implementation of it?

turns.speaker: [speaker uncertain]
paragraphs: [unclear]

turns.speaker: Trent Dilks
paragraphs: Family Leave. I am supportive of [unclear] Family Leave. It has been done. It can be done right. I am critical of our current environment how things are done though. I was talking with a large, he's the CFO of a large business here, and we were really talking about were the businesses in the room, right? Were they in the room for the process? And there are a few things in it that made me think maybe they weren't in the room enough. Also, there has to be a way for the employer to provide input. Right now, they just get the notification. So they don't have a voice in the process. They don't feel like they can provide any feedback. And that needs to be added to it. There's also a provision where I was just talking with a business owner in Paynesville. And where it covers like they had a person who was working 10 hours on average for fund money and that was clearly what they was not to pay the rent it was not for health care it was not to make ends meet this literally was their job so they could go shopping then found out that at 10 hours a week they were eligible for paid family leave so now the small business owner who was trying to make it and barely making it has to pay that out as well. That was not the, I can't believe that was the intention. Now you have to be very careful about when you set the threshold, right? So if you make it 36 hours, Walmart will cap everybody at 35 hours. So you do have to set a threshold high enough that it makes sure that it would be a real pain to screw every worker who needs it the most out of it. But it was not intended for the 10 hour a week so I can go shopping employee. More voices in the room, more business owners in the room who have employees like that, you know, we see it in service industries, stuff like that, I think would have led to that. So the process needs to be more inclusive. Part of that is the other side, whether it's my side, their side, whatever, the other side in general has to stop this pouting, take your ball and go home crap. That is not how good legislation happens. If this is going to be developed and you have the experience and the knowledge to help it be better, it should be your duty in service to try to contribute that. You might not end up voting for the final thing, but you might be able to help improve the process. So that's it as well. I'm supportive of family leave. I believe we need to look at it and revise who it's impacting, how it's impacting, maybe the reach of it. But you shouldn't be one illness away from losing your job, losing your house, losing everything you have. You shouldn't be a family member taking intensive cancer treatments away from losing everything you have. This is the kind of safety net that is appropriate to make sure that we take care of people.

turns.speaker: Aaron Brutger
paragraphs: I opposed to paid family leave. I was prior to it being implemented, and I definitely am now. It puts an unfair burden on small businesses. The company I work for, we have roughly 25 employees. If 10 of us decide to take that leave right now, my employer has to maintain our positions. But how is that going to work? You know, It's not just the company of 25. There are [unclear] small businesses of two people, five people, ten people. It is people we need accountability in general. We need personal accountability and our government needs accountability.

You know, paid leave is something that it used to be a perk of certain employers. We are at a low employment state. You get a job for financial gain and there are also other perks involved. Some companies offer paid leave. You know, when my kids were born, they offered paternity leave. I was able to take that. But I got that job knowing that and knowing that I wanted to start a family. Having the government implement that and put that burden upon small businesses, it's not right. I understand that, and I agree with Trent, people shouldn't be one illness away from losing everything. However, we have other things in place to maintain your job. FMLA has been around for a long time. They will hold your job for you. It just doesn't put the same level of burden on the small company. And the other thing is, with how many people are taking it, with how it was implemented, they're going to have to increase the withholding. The employers are going to have to pay more, and all the workers are going to have to start paying more to pay for it as well. I just, I get the concept of it. I disagree with it fundamentally, and I think how it was rolled out was even worse.

turns.speaker: Angel Zierden
